name: Chambers's Doric Order (overlay on Vignola)
aka: The Attic-based Doric of late Georgian practice

authority.source: William Chambers, A Treatise on Civil Architecture, London 1759, 'Of the Doric Order' and 'Of Pedestals'; expanded 1791 as A Treatise on the Decorative Part of Civil Architecture
authority.author: Sir William Chambers
authority.note: Figures read from the Getty scan of the 1759 first edition, pages 32-35, 44-45, 52 and 82-84. Chambers's Doric is the order in which his comparative method shows best: he sets Fréart's three antique profiles, the Theatre of Marcellus, Palladio, Scamozzi and Vignola against each other and then states which he takes and why.

module.name: The semidiameter of the column at the bottom of the shaft, divided into THIRTY minutes
module.note: Same module as Vignola - the semidiameter - subdivided into thirty minutes instead of twelve parts. Module figures therefore transfer from vignola-doric UNCHANGED; PART figures must be multiplied by 2.5. One Chambers minute is 1/60 of a diameter here and in all four of his other orders, which is the reform that lets his five plates be read against one another. Vignola's Doric part is 1/24 D and his Ionic part is 1/36 D, so nothing in Vignola's Doric can be compared with anything in his Ionic without conversion.

fluting.profile: twenty channels, or the shaft left plain - Chambers: 'the Base is Attic, as in all the Antiques, and the Shaft of the Column may be plain'

members.name: Plinth
members.note: THE HEADLINE DIVERGENCE, AND CHAMBERS NAMES VIGNOLA IN MAKING IT: 'In imitation of Palladio, and all the modern Architects except Vignola, I have made use of the Attic Base in this Order: and it is the most beautiful of any.' He records the alternative fairly first - 'In most of the Antiques, the Doric Column is executed without a Base; Vitruvius likewise makes it without one' - and notes that Scamozzi objected and that the moderns followed Scamozzi. Vignola's Doric base is a torus over a plinth with a bead and apophyge (4 + 5 + 1.5 + 1.5 of 12 parts). Chambers's is the Attic: plinth a third, then two tori with a scotia between. This assembly is restated whole because the member list itself changes, not merely the dimensions.

members.name: Lower torus
members.note: The Attic division: of the two thirds above the plinth, a quarter to the upper torus and of the remainder half to the lower torus and half to the scotia with its fillets. Chambers states in the Corinthian chapter that 'the Base is Attic, and its measures the same as in the Doric and Ionic Orders' - one Attic base serves three of his five orders, which is another economy Vignola does not offer.

members.name: Upper torus
members.note: Chambers adds a rule about base mouldings generally that applies here: their projection should stay under the member above so that the base is sheltered - an argument from weathering rather than from beauty, and the kind of reasoning that makes the Treatise a working book.

members.name: Single fascia
members.note: A MEMBER DROPPED, WITH AN ANTIQUE AUTHORITY GIVEN. Chambers: 'The Architrave is one Module in Height, and composed only of one Fascia and a Fillet, as at the Theatre of Marcellus: the Drops are conical.' Vignola's Doric architrave has TWO fascias plus a regula and a taenia (4 + 4 + 2 + 2 of 12 parts). Chambers reduces it to one broad fascia under the taenia, on the authority of the Theatre of Marcellus, and makes the guttae conical rather than frusto-conical. The result is a plainer, broader architrave that reads as one plane from the ground - which is the Doric argument.

members.name: Taenia
members.note: One sixth of the architrave, the standard figure, with six conical drops hanging below it under each triglyph. The drops overlap the frieze line and are therefore not given a member of their own.

members.name: Base of the pedestal, with its plinth
members.note: Three tenths of the column, against Vignola's third (5 1/3 modules). Chambers records the third as the received maximum and draws his own at three tenths, on the principle that the pedestal is a contrivance for raising the order rather than a member of it. Division nine parts: base 2, dye 6, cornice 1; for a lower pedestal he offers the eight-part division - base 2, dye 5, cornice 1 - 'as Palladio and Perrault' use.

members.name: Cornice or cap of the pedestal

invariants.statement: The module is the semidiameter in thirty minutes, as in all five of Chambers's orders.
The column with capital and base is sixteen modules and the entablature four - Vignola's figures. Chambers keeps the skeleton and changes the members.
The entablature divides into eight: two to the architrave, three to the frieze, three to the cornice. Chambers states this division explicitly; it happens to agree with Vignola exactly.
The pedestal is three tenths of the column, against Vignola's one third.
The Attic base is a full module and its plinth is one third of it.
The diminution begins at the foot of the shaft; there is no cylindrical lower third.

named_spacings.name: chambers-doric-ditriglyph
named_spacings.note: CHAMBERS EXEMPTS THE DORIC FROM HIS OWN EUSTYLE AND SAYS WHY: the Diastyle and Eustyle 'may be employed without distinction in all the Orders, excepting the Doric', because in the Doric 'the most perfect Interval is the Ditriglyph; neither the Monotriglyph, nor the Araeostyle, being to be suffered but in cases of necessity'. The triglyph, not the eye, governs the Doric bay. This is the same conclusion Vignola reaches and it is worth noting that Chambers reaches it by a different route - he argues from the ornament's arithmetic, not from the drawing.

named_spacings.name: chambers-doric-monotriglyph
named_spacings.note: Permitted only 'in cases of necessity'. Chambers's language is stronger than Vignola's, who simply does not draw it.

named_spacings.name: chambers-doric-arcade
named_spacings.note: Chambers records that Vignola's arcade piers 'when the Columns have no Pedestals, are always three Modules, and four, when they have Pedestals', and that Palladio's 'are all of them nearly three Modules and three quarters'. He grades his own by the character of the order - four and a half modules for the Tuscan pier, four for the Corinthian - so the Doric falls near Palladio's figure. Medium confidence: the figure is read from the comparative passage, not from a plate.

derived_rules.note: JUDGMENT SLOT, AND THE CLEAREST STATEMENT OF CHAMBERS'S METHOD: 'I have made the Height of the Doric Column sixteen Modules; which, in buildings where Majesty is required, is a good proportion: but in others it may be slenderer.' In private houses 'it may be 16 1/2, 16 3/4, or 16 7/8 Modules high; and in interior decorations even seventeen Modules'. And the crucial rider: the increase 'may be made entirely on the Shaft, as in the Tuscan Order, without changing either the Base or Capital. The Entablature may remain unaltered: for it will be sufficiently high.' Vignola gives sixteen and nothing else. Chambers gives a band, a criterion (majesty against domesticity) and an instruction on where to take the change.

The upper diameter. Chambers takes one sixth for all five orders - 'seldom less than one eighth of the inferior Diameter of the Column, nor more than one sixth of it' in the antiques, and Vitruvius's one sixth 'esteemed the most perfect'. The FRACTION agrees with Vignola. What does not agree is the origin of the curve: Chambers diminishes from the foot of the shaft by Blondel's conchoid instrument, where Vignola leaves the lower third cylindrical.

JUDGMENT SLOT. Triglyphs in the bay at the ditriglyph interval. Chambers observes elsewhere that 'the distribution of the Dentil-Band will answer pretty nearly in all the regular Intercolumniations' - the point being that dentils forgive and triglyphs do not. The Doric bay must be set out from the triglyph and the fractional remainder taken in the metopes; no formula settles it.

Top width to bottom width. Chambers insists pilasters diminish like columns and is scathing about the contrary opinion. In a Doric pilaster order this matters twice over, because the triglyph is centred on the pilaster and a parallel pilaster throws the triglyph off the axis at the top.

The room as an order. Chambers's Doric entablature divides in eight as 2 : 3 : 3, so the cornice is three eighths; the entablature is a fifth of wall-plus-cornice. 8.1 in at a 9 ft ceiling. The ratio agrees with Vignola; the arithmetic runs in thirtieths, which is why the rule is restated rather than inherited.

The Doric frieze at three eighths of the entablature, carrying triglyphs one module wide and square metopes. Chambers enriches them where Vignola leaves them plain: 'The Metope is enriched with a Bull's skull, adorned with a Garland of Beads; in imitation of those on the Temple of Jupiter Tonans', and the capital's necking 'is enriched with Husks and Roses, as in Palladio's Design, and as it has been executed by Sangallo at the Farnese'. Those enrichments are the visible signature of a Chambers Doric.
Clear span, ditriglyph. Chambers permits neither the araeostyle (weak) nor, except under necessity, the monotriglyph (mean), so the Doric bay is effectively fixed at this one interval.

conflicts.statement: Chambers's Doric costs more than Vignola's in the frieze and less in the architrave. The enriched metopes - bulls' skulls and bead garlands - are a carved item per metope, and a five-bay ditriglyph portico carries upward of twenty of them; the single-fascia architrave, by contrast, is cheaper to run than Vignola's two fascias with regula and taenia.
conflicts.resolution: Take the metope enrichment as a cast repeat from one carved master, which is what the Georgian trade did, and keep the architrave plain as Chambers draws it. If the enrichment is cut, leave the metopes blank rather than substituting a cheap paterae: a blank metope is antique, a bad one is not.

conflicts.statement: The Attic base puts two fillets of 1.25 minutes - 1/48 of a diameter - into the scotia group. At the 6 in default module that is 1/4 in. Cast in GFRC or concrete they will not draw cleanly; in stone they chip.
conflicts.resolution: In cast materials take the fillets to 3/8 in minimum, borrowing from the scotia and recording the deviation on the shop drawing. Do not delete them: a scotia running straight into the tori is what makes a poor Attic base read as a bulge, and Chambers chose this base precisely because it is 'the most beautiful of any'.

conflicts.statement: The ditriglyph bay is 2 3/4 diameters clear with an architrave one module - half a diameter - deep. Chambers rejects wider bays as deficient in strength, which is a correct structural judgement for stone; but modern porticoes are usually framed, and the framer will want to widen the bay to suit joist spans and will take the triglyph spacing with it.
conflicts.resolution: Fix the triglyph pitch first and let the framing follow it. The Doric is the one order whose ornament is load-bearing on the layout: move the bay and every triglyph, mutule and metope in the front moves with it, and there is no way to absorb the error at the corner.

conflicts.statement: Chambers's own rule - that a base's mouldings must project less than the cornice above them, so the base is 'covered and sheltered by it' - is a weathering argument, and it fails in the Attic base of an external Doric in a wet climate, where the scotia holds water and the fillets hold ice.
conflicts.resolution: Slope the scotia's lower fillet outward by two or three degrees and drill a weep at the back of any engaged base. This is invisible at eye level and it is the difference between a stone base that lasts eighty years and one that spalls in twenty.

sources: William Chambers, A Treatise on Civil Architecture, London 1759 (archive.org/details/gri_33125011135288) - pp. 32-35 (diminution), 44-45 (Doric), 52 (column height by building type), 82-85 (pedestals), 88-91 (intercolumniations)
William Chambers, A Treatise on the Decorative Part of Civil Architecture, 3rd ed. London 1791 (archive.org/details/treatiseondecora00cham)
Vignola, Regola delli cinque ordini d'architettura, 1562, as encoded in proportions/orders/vignola-doric.json
Robert Chitham, The Classical Orders of Architecture, 2nd ed. 2005
notes:
THE FOUR DELTAS, EACH WITH CHAMBERS'S REASON ATTACHED. (1) THE ATTIC BASE, in imitation of Palladio 'and all the modern Architects except Vignola' - the one place where Chambers names Vignola as the outlier and departs from him deliberately. (2) THE SINGLE-FASCIA ARCHITRAVE after the Theatre of Marcellus, with conical drops, replacing Vignola's two fascias and regula. (3) THE PEDESTAL at three tenths rather than a third, divided nine parts as 2 : 6 : 1. (4) THE DIMINUTION beginning at the foot of the shaft by Blondel's conchoid, not from a cylindrical lower third - the fraction, one sixth, being unchanged. Add the module's uniform thirtieths and the column-height band (16 for majesty, up to 17 for interiors, the increase taken wholly on the shaft) and the Doric is fully described.

WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED. The capital and the cornice. The Getty OCR of p. 45 reads Chambers's Doric capital as thirty-two minutes, which would be two minutes taller than Vignola's module-high capital and would have to be taken out of the shaft. That is a single OCR reading of an eighteenth-century long-s text, it is not corroborated by any second source reached, and encoding it would propagate a possible error into both the capital and the shaft. It is therefore recorded here as a note and NOT encoded; a reader with access to a clean copy of the Treatise should check it. The cornice's individual mouldings are on the plate only and are illegible in every scan reached; no members are invented for them, and they inherit from vignola-doric subject to the 2.5x part conversion.

THE ENTABLATURE AGREES WITH VIGNOLA AND CHAMBERS SAYS SO ARITHMETICALLY: four modules 'divided into eight parts, two of them are for the Architrave, three for the Frize, and three for the Cornice'. It is worth recording an agreement this exact, because it shows that Chambers's departures are deliberate and local rather than a wholesale rewriting.
